newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's key Cetes rate surprises with large jump.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's key Cetes rate surprises with large jump.

text.p: Mexico's bellwether one-month Cetes rate continued its steep climb on Tuesday, the central bank said, as the recent 10-week slide in interest rates faded into a distant memory.

Rising interest rates in the secondary money market and at Banco de Mexico's primary auction reflected concerns that the Federal Open Market Comittee might opt to raise U.S. interest rates later this month, analysts said.
A weaker peso has helped push up local interest rates, a trend that started at last week's auction when the 28-day Cetes rate shot up 257 basis points.
This week the one-month paper rose a sharp 201 basis points to yield 23.17 percent.
A survey of nine money market dealers by Reuters earlier in the day found expectations of a rise of only 93 basis points on the one-month paper.
"There was a little bit of nervousness in the market near term, specifically over the direction of U.S. markets," said MMS International analyst Scott Grimberg.
Demand slipped sharply for the 28-day paper at the auction, with only 1.03 billion pesos worth demanded for the 800 million pesos on offer.
However, in a clear sign that worries about inflation are declining, the yield curve has flattened out.
At the primary auction, the rate on the three-month paper rose only five basis points to 22.86 percent, while the six-month paper rate showed a decline of 16 basis points to 23.17 percent.
The yield on one-year paper was 24.22 percent this week compared to 24.49 percent the week before.
By late February rates had fallen to their lowest levels since the 1994 peso crash as investors were cheered by good economic news out of Mexico, particularly waning inflationary pressures.
Rates had fallen by almost 1,000 basis points in two months, dropping much faster and further than observers had expected.
The peso, however, was kept stable on heavy inflows of capital into Mexico's markets.
But, as happens often enough in Mexico's volatile markets, the primary interest rates had fallen too far and peso volatility may have knocked them back higher, analysts said.
In a recent report, Salomon Brothers said that investors should be wary of Mexican local-denominated paper.

"An underweight allocation is, however, suggested with respect to Mexican local currency instruments, given the real risk of a further step wise jump in the currency within the next two months," it said in an emerging markets report.
Demand has also been variable. Two weeks ago it tumbled to 7.82 billion pesos. Then last week demand rose to 12.06 billion pesos.
This week, however, demand remained strong at 12.14 billion pesos.
But most of the demand was centered on the 182-day and 357-day paper, with bid-to-cover ratios of 6.26 and 4.86, respectively.
